'''Samuel Thornton Durrance''' (September 17, 1943 – May 5, 2023) was an American scientist who flew aboard two [[NASA]] [[Space Shuttle]] missions as a [[payload specialist]].

==Background==
Durrance was born September 17, 1943, in [[Tallahassee, Florida]], but grew up in [[Tampa, Florida]].<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=http://astronautix.com/d/durrance.html|title=Durrance|date=December 28, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228020032/http://astronautix.com/d/durrance.html |archive-date=December 28, 2016 }}</ref> He attended Wilson Junior High and graduated from [[Plant High School]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tuchman |first=Alma |date=July 27, 1984 |title=Durrance is going to go |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k8w_AAAAIBAJ&dq=%22Durrance+attended+Wilson+Junior+High+and+Plant+High+School%22&pg=PA19 |publisher=Lakeland Ledger |via=Google Books}}</ref> in 1961, lettering in [[American football]] for three years and playing both defense and offense.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |date=January 1, 1990 |title=Florida physicist to fly on Columbia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kisTAAAAIBAJ&dq=%22Samuel+T.+Durrance%22&pg=PA10 |publisher=Ocala Star-Banner |via=Google Books}}</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree and a [[Master of Science]] degree in [[physics]] (with honors), at [[California State University, Los Angeles]] (Cal State LA), 1972 and 1974, respectively,<ref name="auto"/> and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree in astro-geophysics at the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]], 1980.<ref name="auto1"/> In 2000, he was awarded an Honorary Doctor of Science from the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]] along with eight other astronaut alums.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2000-04-27 |title=Nine CU Astronaut-Alums To Receive Honorary Degrees At Commencement |url=https://www.colorado.edu/today/2000/04/27/nine-cu-astronaut-alums-receive-honorary-degrees-commencement |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=CU Boulder Today |language=en}}</ref>

Durrance was a principal [[Research Scientist|research scientist]] in the Department of Physics and [[Astronomy]] at [[Johns Hopkins University]], Baltimore, Maryland.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Samuel T. Durrance |url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/durrance.pdf |website=NASA.gov}}</ref> He was a co-investigator for the [[Hopkins Ultraviolet Telescope]], one of the instruments of the Astro [[Space observatory|Observatory]].<ref name=":0" />

Beginning in 2001, he was the executive director of the [[Florida Space Research Institute]] which was located at the NASA [[Kennedy Space Center]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Samuel Durrance, astronaut who flew with telescope he built, dies at 79 |url=http://www.collectspace.com/news/news-050523a-astronaut-samuel-durrance-obituary.html |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=collectSPACE.com}}</ref>

Durrance resided in [[Melbourne, Florida]], and was a professor of physics and space sciences at [[Florida Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{Cite web |first=Jon |last=Schroeder |date=2023-05-10 |title=Samuel Durrance, enterprising astronomer and space researcher, dies at 79 |url=https://hub.jhu.edu/2023/05/10/samuel-durrance-obituary/ |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=The Hub |language=en}}</ref>

Durrance was a member of the [[American Astronomical Society]], [[American Geophysical Union]], [[International Astronomical Union]], [[Association of Space Explorers]], [[Planetary Society]], and [[Phi Kappa Phi]].<ref name="auto"/>

==Academic career==
[[File:S035 lesson hoffman durrance.jpg|thumb|right|240px|Sam Durrance and Jeffrey Hoffman during the first classroom lesson broadcast from space]]
Durrance had been involved in the flight hardware development, [[optical]] and [[mechanics|mechanical]] design, [[construction]], and integration of the Hopkins Ultraviolet Telescope and the Astro Observatory,<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=z-M-YksXsqcC&dq=%22Samuel+T.+Durrance%22+-wikipedia&pg=PA437|title=Who's who of NASA Astronauts|first=Lee|last=Ellis|date=May 12, 2004|publisher=Americana Group Publishing|isbn=9780966796148 |via=Google Books}}</ref> and had conducted research and directed graduate students at the Johns Hopkins University<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/durrance.pdf|title=Payload Specialist Bio: Dr. Samuel T. Durrance 5/96|access-date=January 19, 2021|archive-date=June 4, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200604020602/https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/durrance.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> He had designed and built [[spectrometer]]s, detectors, and [[Reprography|imaging]] systems, and made numerous [[spacecraft]] and ground-based astronomical observations. He conceived and directed a program at Johns Hopkins University to develop adaptive-optics instrumentation for ground-based astronomy. He led the team that designed and constructed the Adaptive Optics [[Coronagraph]], which led to the discovery of the first cool [[brown dwarf]] orbiting a nearby star. He was also a co-discoverer of changes in the planet-forming disk surrounding the star [[beta Pictoris]].

In March 1986,<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 30, 1986 |title=Flight delayed |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8Z4_AAAAIBAJ&dq=%22Samuel+T.+Durrance%22&pg=PA22 |publisher=The Vindicator |via=Google Books}}</ref> Durrance's first mission was for [[STS-61-E]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.spacefacts.de/bios/astronauts/english/durrance_samuel.htm|title=Astronaut Biography: Samuel Durrance|website=www.spacefacts.de|access-date=February 25, 2022|archive-date=December 4, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211204230820/http://www.spacefacts.de/bios/astronauts/english/durrance_samuel.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> It was canceled after the [[Challenger disaster]].<ref name="auto"/> Durrance logged over 615 hours in space as a [[payload specialist]] and member of the crew of [[Space Shuttle Columbia|Space Shuttle ''Columbia'']] for the [[STS-35]]/Astro-1 and [[Space Shuttle Endeavour|Space Shuttle ''Endeavour'']] for the [[STS-67]]/Astro-2 missions.<ref name="auto2"/>

==Later assignment (2006)==
[[Image:STS035-49-028 - STS-35 payload specialists perform balancing act on OV-102's middeck - 1990.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Payload Specialists Durrance and Parise work out.]]
Durrance was employed by the [[Florida Institute of Technology]] in Melbourne, Florida, serving as a professor in the Department of Aerospace, Physics and Space Sciences.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aerospace, Physics and Space Sciences |url=https://www.fit.edu/aerospace-physics-and-space-sciences/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230315170432/https://www.fit.edu/aerospace-physics-and-space-sciences/ |archive-date=March 15, 2023 |access-date=May 12, 2023 |website=www.fit.edu}}</ref>

==Illness and death==
Durrance was diagnosed with [[Alzheimer's disease]] in 2021. He died at a hospice facility in [[Viera, Florida]], on May 5, 2023, of complications from a fall, after battling dementia and [[Parkinson's disease]]. He was 79.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sam Durrance, astronaut who flew with telescope he built, dies at 79 |url=http://www.collectspace.com/news/news-050523a-astronaut-samuel-durrance-obituary.html |website=CollectSpace |access-date=May 5, 2023 |archive-date=May 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505190016/http://www.collectspace.com/news/news-050523a-astronaut-samuel-durrance-obituary.html |url-status=live }}</ref>
